paragraphs.heading: Solid rock that slowly flows
paragraphs.text: Mantle convection is the extremely slow creeping motion of Earth's mantle, which is made of solid silicate rock. As this rock creeps, currents carry heat from deep inside the planet up toward the surface. It works a little like a pot of thick soup on a stove, except that the 'soup' is solid stone. This slow churning is what drives the tectonic plates across Earth's surface.

paragraphs.heading: Where plates are made
paragraphs.text: The lithosphere rides on top of the asthenosphere, and together these two layers make up the upper mantle. The lithosphere is broken into plates that are always being built at some edges and destroyed at others. At spreading centres on the seafloor, mantle material is added to the growing edge of a plate. The hot new rock then loses heat as it travels away from where it formed.

paragraphs.heading: Where plates sink
paragraphs.text: By the time a plate reaches its far edge, its rock has cooled, shrunk and grown dense. It then sinks under its own weight, usually at an ocean trench, in a process called subduction. Subduction is the downward half of mantle convection. Some of this sinking material seems to reach the lower mantle, while elsewhere something stops it from going deeper.

paragraphs.heading: Layered or whole
paragraphs.text: In the late 20th century, geophysicists argued over whether the mantle churns in separate layers or as one whole. Evidence from seismic tomography, along with computer simulations and studies of Earth's gravity, now leans toward whole-mantle convection. In that picture, cold sinking plates fall all the way to the boundary with the core. Hot plumes rise from that boundary all the way back to the surface.

paragraphs.heading: How fast and how long
paragraphs.text: At the surface, this motion shows up as plates moving a few centimetres per year. Flow can be quicker in runny zones just under the lithosphere and slower in the stiffer lowest mantle. One shallow loop of convection takes around 50 million years, while a deeper loop may take nearer 200 million. The mantle's Rayleigh number is estimated at around 10⁷, a value that points to vigorous convection.

paragraphs.heading: Today's pattern
paragraphs.text: Today, broad sinking flow is thought to lie beneath the Americas and the western Pacific, both places with a long history of subduction. Rising flow lies beneath the central Pacific and Africa. Plate motions match this, with plates converging toward the western Pacific and the Americas and spreading away from Africa and the central Pacific. Because that spreading away from Africa and the Pacific has lasted for 250 million years, the overall flow pattern appears to be stable over the long term.
